correctness.rationale: The reverse-triangle inequality forces every zero with r^(n−k)≤c/2 into the bounded inner rescaling; the complementary outer rescaling is bounded above and bounded away from zero. Every subsequential limit is therefore among the relevant polygon vertices. Their real Jacobians are −k^2 and n^2−k^2 in the rescaled equations, so analytic implicit-function uniqueness both continues all vertices and excludes any extra branches. Linearization gives −omega^(1−n)/k for the inner correction and n h−k conjugate(h)=epsilon_o zeta^(−n) to first order for the outer one. For all c>0 the lower phase equality forces both phases to be 1 and hence the positive real root by coprimality. For the upper radius its scalar equation has exactly one solution above R, and equality needs phases +1 and −1; this forces the negative real point if n is even and is impossible if n is odd. In odd degree n is invertible mod 2(n+k); the leading radial correction has a two-way maximum at phases plus or minus pi/(n+k), separated from the other values by a fixed gap. Conjugacy makes the two resulting root moduli exactly equal. Expanding U_c and subtracting on this same outer scale gives the two stated powers and the positive coefficient, with n,k fixed.
residual_risks: The numerical checks are finite and neither give root exhaustion nor supply a uniform threshold. The analytic proof asserts the odd-degree farthest pair for sufficiently large c for each fixed exponent pair, not all c.

value.rationale: This answers the large-parameter part of a previously posed location problem, replacing a count and enclosure with exact local branch labels and the rate and coefficient by which the enclosure misses every root in odd degree. The odd/even split also specifies which actual roots extremize rather than merely restating an annular bound.
residual_risks: This contribution is asymptotic, not a complete all-parameter geometry or a certified coefficient threshold.
